title: NASA's Twin ESCAPADE Probes Slingshot Past Earth This Morning on a First-of-Its-Kind Trip to Mars
excerpt: NASA's twin ESCAPADE spacecraft performed a first-of-its-kind powered flyby of Earth early this morning, firing their engines at closest approach to…
content:
NASA's two ESCAPADE spacecraft performed a first-of-its-kind "powered" flyby of Earth early this morning, combining Earth's gravity with an engine burn to slingshot toward Mars — a maneuver no agency spacecraft has flown before, according to NASA.

The first spacecraft's flyby and engine burn took place around 5 a.m. EST on Saturday, Nov. 7. The second follows around 6 a.m. EST on Monday, Nov. 9, according to NASA Science.

At closest approach, each spacecraft performs a "trans-Mars injection burn," firing its engine for about 9 minutes, according to NASA. The burn raises each spacecraft's speed by more than 1,000 mph — from about 6.3 to about 6.7 miles per second, or about Mach 30 to Mach 31. At that speed, a spacecraft could fly from Washington, D.C., to San Francisco in under 7 minutes.

After the flybys, the probes begin a 10-month cruise to Mars, arriving Sept. 7 and Sept. 9, 2027, respectively, according to NASA. At Mars, ESCAPADE — the Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers — will be the first multi-spacecraft mission to fly in formation around the planet, studying how the solar wind strips away the Martian atmosphere.

A new route to Mars

ESCAPADE launched in November 2025, when Earth and Mars were on opposite sides of the Sun. Instead of heading straight to Mars, the probes looped around the Earth-Sun Lagrange point 2 and came back to Earth to use its gravity — a new route, since Mars launch windows normally come only every 26 months, according to NASA.

Each spacecraft is about the size of a standard refrigerator and passed between 600 and 1,100 miles above Earth's surface — higher than most Earth-orbiting satellites, according to NASA. The engine burns happen over southern Australia; the first burn began at 4:51 a.m. EST. The probes were brightest for the western United States between midnight and 1 a.m. PST on Nov. 7, and will be again from 1 to 2 a.m. PST on Nov. 9 — though a telescope is most likely needed to spot them, according to NASA and EarthSky.

The two probes, nicknamed Blue and Gold for UC Berkeley's school colors, were built by Rocket Lab and launched aboard Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket on Nov. 13, 2025, from Cape Canaveral, according to EarthSky.

What is not yet confirmed

The success of today's burn has not yet been confirmed. NASA said the team will know how well the spacecraft are aimed for Mars several days after the burns, with trajectory corrections to follow. This story will be updated when NASA confirms the results of the flybys.
